title: When the Clock Sings
premise: In the winter of 1899, during a colonial war the newspapers refuse to name honestly, battlefield nurse Lena Voss keeps a private ledger of soldiers whose deaths officers have recorded as desertion, disease, or nothing at all. When the army requisitions her garrison town and seizes all official records, Lena realizes her ledger is the only surviving account of forty-one men — and that Major Aldous Crane, who once loved her, is the officer charged with writing the campaign's official history. As Crane closes in on the ledger and on her, Lena must choose between protecting the man she still loves and delivering the truth to a journalist smuggling documents out before the century turns. She testifies at a quiet court of inquiry, loses Crane to his duty, and ends the book on New Year's Eve, 1900, reading her names aloud in the town square as the new century's first bell rings.
about_author: Orsen Galloway is the pen name of a former archivist who spent a decade cataloguing military correspondence from forgotten colonial campaigns. When the Clock Sings is a debut novel born from a single misfiled ledger found behind a drawer in a provincial records office.

chapters.title: The Ledger Under the Floorboard
chapters.summary: Lena Voss, POV. In a muddy field hospital, Lena records the death of Private Ellery Shaw, officially logged as 'deserted,' and adds him to her hidden ledger of erased men. The emotional beat is quiet defiance: she cannot save them, but she can remember them.

chapters.title: Requisition Orders
chapters.summary: Lena, POV. The army announces it will occupy the town and seize all civilian and medical records for the official campaign history. Lena watches clerks crate documents while her ledger burns against her ribs like a coal. The beat is dread sharpening into resolve.

chapters.title: Major Crane Arrives
chapters.summary: Lena, POV. Major Aldous Crane, the historian-officer, steps off the transport — the man she nursed through fever two years ago and never stopped thinking about. Their reunion is courteous, careful, and loaded. The beat is love rekindling against her better judgment.

chapters.title: Forty-One Names
chapters.summary: Crane, POV. Crane begins reconstructing the campaign and notices gaps: men unaccounted for, reports that contradict muster rolls. He suspects clerical error, not cover-up. The beat is professional unease — the first crack in his faith in the army's record.

chapters.title: What the Orderly Saw
chapters.summary: Lena, POV. A dying orderly whispers that Captain Brice ordered wounded prisoners abandoned at Kessel Ford, then falsified the returns. Lena writes it down, hands shaking. The beat is the moment remembering becomes dangerous.

chapters.title: Dinner with the Enemy of My Heart
chapters.summary: Crane, POV. Crane invites Lena to advise on hospital records; over candlelight they circle old affection and new silences. He mentions the missing forty-one; she says nothing. The beat is intimacy built on a secret, and how heavy that makes every smile.

chapters.title: The Burning Cart
chapters.summary: Lena, POV. Soldiers burn 'redundant' paperwork in the yard; among the flames Lena glimpses pages bearing Kessel Ford dates. She understands the history is being written by arson. The beat is grief curdling into purpose.

chapters.title: Sister Agnes's Warning
chapters.summary: Lena, POV. Matron Agnes, who has survived three wars, tells Lena that women who keep accounts get accounted for. She offers to hide the ledger in the convent. The beat is loyalty tested — trust another woman, or trust no one.

chapters.title: Brice Takes Notice
chapters.summary: Crane, POV. Captain Brice, charming and lethal, warns Crane off 'hospital gossip' and arranges a promotion that would send him home early. Crane declines without knowing why he does. The beat is temptation of comfort versus the itch of truth.

chapters.title: A Search Warranted
chapters.summary: Lena, POV. Brice orders a search of the hospital quarters 'for contraband correspondence.' Lena moves the ledger into a hymnal box in the chapel hours ahead of the soldiers. The beat is near-catastrophe and the cost of constant fear.

chapters.title: The Question He Shouldn't Ask
chapters.summary: Crane, POV. Crane finds a discrepancy only someone present at Kessel Ford could know, and asks Lena directly whether she was there. She lies. He sees the lie. Neither names it. The beat is love and suspicion entwining until they are indistinguishable.

chapters.title: Ellery's Mother
chapters.summary: Lena, POV. A letter arrives from Ellery Shaw's mother asking how her son truly died. Lena drafts four replies and burns them all. The beat is the human weight of the ledger — each name a family waiting.

chapters.title: The Journalist in the Coal Cellar
chapters.summary: Lena, POV. Lena meets Tomas Reik, a foreign correspondent hiding in the coal cellar of the tavern, who can smuggle documents past the cordon if she can get them to him. The beat is hope arriving disguised as recklessness.

chapters.title: Copy of a Copy
chapters.summary: Lena, POV. Over three sleepless nights Lena copies the ledger and her testimony onto tissue paper, hiding originals with Sister Agnes. The beat is quiet heroism — the work of truth is tedious, terrified, and steady.

chapters.title: Betrayal at the Infirmary Gate
chapters.summary: Crane, POV. An informant reports a nurse is passing papers; Crane must lead the search himself. He finds nothing but knows, absolutely, what he has chosen not to find. The beat is complicity — loyalty beginning to outweigh obedience.

chapters.title: Brice's Bargain
chapters.summary: Lena, POV. Brice corners Lena alone and offers amnesty for the ledger and silence about her 'association' with Crane — if she surrenders it tonight. She refuses. The beat is open war declared, and terror walked through with a straight spine.

chapters.title: Arrest
chapters.summary: Crane, POV. Brice arrests Lena for theft of official property, using Crane's own search report as evidence. Crane realizes he has been the instrument all along. The beat is devastation — the moment duty shows its true face.

chapters.title: The Court of Inquiry
chapters.summary: Lena, POV. At a closed inquiry, Lena testifies to all forty-one names from memory, having surrendered only the decoy copy hidden in the hymnal box. Her voice steadies as she speaks. The beat is the climax: truth spoken aloud, finally, on the record.

chapters.title: Crane Breaks Ranks
chapters.summary: Crane, POV. Called to corroborate the charges, Crane instead presents his own reconstructed evidence of Kessel Ford, destroying his career in eleven minutes of testimony. The beat is sacrifice — love expressed as truth rather than protection.

chapters.title: Verdicts
chapters.summary: Lena, POV. Brice is quietly retired, not tried; the findings are sealed 'in the national interest.' Lena is released, her ledger returned, her victory half a victory. The beat is bitter clarity about what institutions do with truth.

chapters.title: The Smuggled Pages
chapters.summary: Lena, POV. Weeks later, Reik's dispatch appears in foreign papers naming all forty-one men; copies circulate hand to hand in the town. Families write to Lena. Crane, stripped of rank, chooses to stay. The beat is mourning and unexpected grace.

chapters.title: When the Clock Sings
chapters.summary: Lena, POV. On New Year's Eve, 1900, the town gathers at the churchyard as Lena reads the forty-one names aloud and the century's first bell drowns and then carries them. Crane stands beside her, no longer an officer, just a man. The beat is belonging earned at last — memory outliving empire.
